title: Mawlid: the Prophet's birth
hookLine: many Muslims celebrate the Prophet's birth with poems and gatherings in Rabi' al-Awwal, while others don't mark it

lines: CITIES LIT UP, AND QUIET HOUSES.
cards: Someone once asked the Prophet ﷺ why he fasted on Mondays. His answer, recorded in Muslim's collection, was short: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation first came to me.
It's the clearest word in the hadith on how he himself marked the day: he fasted. Centuries later, in the third month of the Islamic year, Rabi' al-Awwal, whole cities light up for it.
And other Muslims, just as devoted to him, don't mark the day at all. Today, the Mawlid.

teach.b: Mawlid means birth, or the time and place of a birth, from the root w-l-d, to give birth. Sunni communities often mark it on the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, and Shia communities often on the seventeenth.
The sources don't settle the exact date. Public celebrations grew up over the centuries.

teach.h: POEMS, LIGHTS, FOOD FOR THE POOR.
teach.b: Historians point to the Fatimid court in Cairo, and to Irbil in northern Iraq in the early 1200s, where a ruler named Muzaffar al-Din held huge gatherings with recitations and food for the poor.
Today, in places from Morocco to Indonesia, people gather to recite poems in the Prophet's praise. Some sing the Burda, the Mantle, by the Egyptian poet al-Busiri.
Others recite mawlid texts that tell his birth and life in verse. Mosques are decorated. Sweets are handed out.

Some scholars, notably in the Salafi tradition, say that since the companions didn't hold such gatherings, the day shouldn't be made a festival, and they keep their love for the Prophet in following his example every day.
Supporters answer that remembering him with joy and praise is good, even if the form is new. The disagreement is real, and serious people stand on both sides.
What both sides share is the salawat. Surah Al-Ahzab says: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation."
And a hadith in Muslim says that whoever sends one blessing on the Prophet, God sends ten blessings on them. On the Mawlid or on any ordinary Monday, that blessing is one way Muslims keep him close.

how: Many Muslims mark the Mawlid in Rabi' al-Awwal with gatherings, poetry such as the Burda, and charity, while others, following scholars who regard it as a later practice, do not celebrate it; nearly all send blessings on the Prophet.

games.q: someone asks the Prophet why he fasts on Mondays. what does he say?
o: it's the day the Ka'ba was rebuilt.
it's the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me.
it's the day the week begins.
games.why: the day I was born, and the day revelation first came to me. it's the clearest word in the hadith on how he himself marked the day.

practice: If you pray, say a blessing on the Prophet ten times, slowly; many Muslims use the short form, sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam, may God bless him and give him peace.
If you don't pray, spend the time with one thing from the Prophet's life, learned on this path, that stayed with you.

wordCard.voice: Mawlid. The Prophet's birth, celebrated by many Muslims with poems and gatherings in Rabi' al-Awwal, and left unmarked by others. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: mawlid, birth or birthday, from the root w-l-d.

carryVoice: Your line: peace on the one born. Lit streets or quiet houses, the blessing is shared. Day five hundred five, done.
